pairs.rationale: Both accounts place Jesus beside the sea before the parable teaching; Mark also describes the crowd and boat in this verse.
Both describe the large crowd, Jesus sitting in a boat, and the crowd remaining on the land beside the sea.
Both introduce teaching in parables and begin with the sower going out to sow.
Both versions describe seed beside the road being eaten by birds.
Both describe seed springing up quickly on rocky ground because the soil is shallow.
Both describe the sun scorching the plants and their withering because they have no root.
Both describe growing thorns choking the seed; Mark also explicitly states that it produced no fruit.
Both describe good soil yielding thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold, although the order of the yields is reversed.
Both conclude the sower parable with the summons for the person with ears to hear.
Both place a question about the parables among Jesus' followers. Matthew gives the question why He speaks in parables; Mark describes their asking about the parables when He was alone.
Both contrast the disciples' received knowledge of the kingdom's mystery with the use of parables for those outside.
Both state that whoever has will receive more, while whoever does not have will lose even what he has; Matthew adds abundance.

Both connect parable teaching with seeing without seeing and hearing without understanding. Matthew gives this as the reason He speaks in parables, whereas Mark phrases it as so that; the causal wording is not harmonized.
Matthew explicitly calls this Isaiah's prophecy and quotes the warning about repeated hearing without understanding and repeated seeing without perception.
Both describe the people's dull or fattened heart, difficult hearing, closed eyes, and the possibility of turning and being healed. The vocabulary differs slightly in this supplied English edition.
Both pronounce the disciples' seeing eyes blessed. Matthew also mentions their hearing ears; Luke's cited verse mentions the eyes.
Both describe earlier people longing to see and hear what the disciples now experience. Matthew names prophets and righteous people, whereas Luke names prophets and kings.

Matthew introduces the sower explanation by calling the disciples to hear it; Mark introduces the explanation with a question about their understanding and then identifies the sowing as sowing the word.
Both interpret the roadside seed as hearers from whom the evil one or Satan takes away the sown word; Matthew additionally stresses lack of understanding.
Both identify the rocky-ground hearers as those who immediately receive the word with joy.
Both describe rootless hearers lasting only briefly and stumbling when distress or persecution arises because of the word.
Both interpret the thorns as cares and the deceitfulness of riches choking the heard word until it is unfruitful. Mark additionally mentions desires for other things.

Both identify the good-soil hearers by their fruitful reception of the word and the thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold yields. Matthew says understanding and Mark says accepting; the yield order also differs.
The later explanation identifies the sower of the good seed in this same chapter's parable as the Son of Man. This is an explicit link between the parable and its interpretation.
The same chapter's explanation identifies the darnel as sons of the evil one and the enemy who sowed it as the devil; it explains the hostile sowing described here.
The later explanation distinguishes the good seed as sons of the kingdom and the darnel as sons of the evil one, explaining the two growths that become visible in this parable.

The householder's slaves ask how darnel arose despite good sowing; the later explanation identifies the good sower, good seed, darnel, and hostile devil who sowed it. It supplies the parable's interpretive identities.

The explanation identifies the enemy blamed here as the devil and relates the harvest and reapers to the consummation and angels; the slaves' proposal to gather the darnel is not itself repeated there.

The later explanation interprets the harvest as the age's consummation, the reapers as angels, and the burning of gathered darnel as judgment. This is the same parable's explanation rather than an independent event.
Both compare the kingdom with a mustard seed being sown; Matthew says the kingdom of the heavens and Mark the kingdom of God.

Both describe the small mustard seed growing beyond the garden plants and providing a place for birds; Matthew describes a tree and resting in branches, whereas Mark describes great branches and shelter under their shade.
Both compare the kingdom to a woman hiding leaven in three sata of flour until the whole is leavened.
Both summarize Jesus' public use of parables and state that He did not speak to them without a parable. Mark additionally describes private explanation to the disciples.

Matthew's fulfillment citation shares the psalm's opening of the mouth in parables and utterance of ancient hidden material. The psalm says riddles from the beginning, while Matthew says things hidden from the foundation of the world; this edition numbers the psalm 77.

Matthew describes disciples privately requesting an explanation after Jesus leaves the crowds; Mark summarizes His private explanation of parables to His own disciples. Mark does not name the darnel parable or the house here.
Jesus identifies the Son of Man as the good sower from the parable introduced earlier in this chapter; the source gives the interpretive identity for that earlier image.
This explanation identifies the field, good seed, and darnel from the preceding parable as the world, sons of the kingdom, and sons of the evil one.

This explanation identifies the enemy, harvest, and reapers in the earlier parable as the devil, the consummation of the age, and angels. The earlier command to wait for harvest supplies its narrative setting.
The source explicitly interprets the earlier gathering and burning of the darnel as an image of the consummation of the age.
Both explanations of judgment parables describe angels separating or gathering the wicked from among those belonging to the kingdom; the darnel and dragnet remain different images.
The two parable explanations repeat the furnace of fire and the weeping and grinding of teeth as the fate of the wicked.

Matthew's righteous shining like the sun recalls Daniel's understanding people appearing like heaven's lights and those strengthening his words like stars. This is an illuminating-light comparison, with Daniel's supplied Greek-based wording retained rather than replaced by another edition.

The parable's man sells his possessions for the treasure-bearing field; Jesus elsewhere calls the rich man to sell his belongings, give to the poor, receive heavenly treasure, and follow Him. The connection is costly pursuit of kingdom treasure, without equating the two transactions.

These neighboring kingdom parables use valued material objects, fine pearls and hidden treasure, to portray the kingdom's worth. The merchant's search differs from the other man's discovery of a field's treasure.
Both kingdom parables describe selling everything to obtain the discovered object of great value, a pearl in this verse and a treasure-bearing field in the other.

The dragnet's gathering of every kind of fish can be compared with the field parable's mixed world of sons of the kingdom and sons of the evil one. These are distinct parable images whose subsequent explanations describe separation at the consummation.

Both parables distinguish a retained good yield from a rejected bad yield: good fish are gathered while rotten fish are discarded, and wheat is stored while darnel is burned. The disposal imagery differs.
Both explanations describe angels carrying out the separation or gathering of evil at the consummation; the source belongs to the dragnet explanation and the target to the darnel explanation.
The dragnet explanation repeats the darnel explanation's furnace of fire, weeping, and grinding of teeth.

The disciples' affirmation that they understand these teachings can be read alongside Jesus' earlier statement that knowledge of the kingdom's mysteries has been given to them. The link concerns this chapter's contrast in understanding, not a second report of this question.
Both hometown accounts describe synagogue teaching and astonished questions about Jesus' wisdom and mighty works.

Both hometown questions name Mary and Jesus' brothers. Matthew calls Him the craftsman's son; Mark calls Him the carpenter. Matthew's Joseph and Mark's Joses are retained as each edition's wording rather than silently harmonized.
Both hometown objections refer to Jesus' sisters living among the townspeople; Matthew also repeats their question about the source of His abilities.
Both accounts describe offense at Jesus and His saying that a prophet lacks honor in his hometown and household; Mark additionally mentions relatives.

Both connect the restricted mighty works in Jesus' hometown with unbelief. Matthew says He did not do many; Mark says He could do no mighty work except healing a few sick people and then marvels at their unbelief.
Both introduce Herod hearing the report about Jesus as His name becomes known; Matthew calls him tetrarch and Mark king.

Both associate reports of Jesus' powers with the claim that John has risen. Matthew puts the claim about resurrection and powers directly in Herod's speech; Mark first reports it as what people said and later records Herod identifying the risen John whom he beheaded.
Both explain John's arrest, binding, and imprisonment through Herod's relationship with Herodias, identified as his brother Philip's wife.
Both record John's repeated objection that Herod's possession of his brother's wife is unlawful.

Both passages describe fear of the crowd because the people regard John as a prophet. Here the fear restrains Herod; in the later passage it shapes the authorities' response to Jesus about John's baptism.

Both place the pleasing dance at Herod's birthday celebration. Matthew calls the dancer Herodias's daughter, whereas this supplied Mark text calls her his daughter Herodias; that difference is preserved without resolving her parentage.
Both describe Herod swearing to give the girl what she asks; Mark additionally states the promise extends up to half his kingdom.
Both connect the mother's instruction with the girl's request for John the Baptist's head on a platter; Mark narrates the consultation and request separately.
Both describe the king's grief and his unwillingness to refuse because of his oaths and the guests reclining with him.
Both report Herod ordering John's beheading in prison; Mark identifies the messenger as an executioner.
Both narrate John's head being brought on a platter, given to the girl, and passed by her to her mother.
Both describe John's disciples taking his corpse for burial. Matthew additionally reports their subsequent visit to tell Jesus.

Both describe the private boat withdrawal to a deserted place and crowds traveling there on foot from the cities. Matthew links the withdrawal to news of John's death, whereas Mark's preceding context concerns the apostles' return and rest.

Both describe Jesus emerging, seeing the great crowd, and being moved with compassion. Matthew follows with healing; Mark explains the compassion through sheep without a shepherd and follows with teaching.
Both disciples point to the deserted location and late hour and ask Jesus to dismiss the crowds to buy food in nearby settlements.
Both give Jesus' instruction that the disciples themselves provide food; Mark also records their question about the cost of buying bread.
Both identify the available food as five loaves and two fish, although Mark places the answer after Jesus tells the disciples to check the supply.

Both describe reclining on grass and Jesus taking the five loaves and two fish, looking heavenward, blessing, breaking, and distributing through the disciples. Mark additionally describes the seated groups.
Both state that everyone ate and was satisfied and that twelve baskets of fragments were collected.
Both count the eaters as about five thousand men; Matthew explicitly adds that women and children are outside that count.
Both describe Jesus compelling the disciples to go ahead by boat while He dismisses the crowd; Mark additionally names Bethsaida as their direction.
Both describe Jesus withdrawing to the mountain to pray and being alone when evening comes.
Both describe the disciples' boat being hindered by an opposing wind; Matthew emphasizes waves and distance from land, whereas Mark describes their strained rowing.
Both place Jesus' approach while walking on the sea around the fourth watch of the night.
Both describe the disciples mistaking Jesus' sea-walking appearance for a phantom or apparition and crying out in fear.
Both record Jesus immediately reassuring them with the commands to take courage and not fear and the words it is I.

Peter's cry for the Lord to save him in danger on the water resembles the disciples' earlier plea for the Lord to save them while they feared perishing at sea. These are different episodes, and the earlier passage does not describe Peter walking.
Both sea episodes connect fear with Jesus' rebuke of little faith. Here He grasps Peter and asks why he doubted; in the earlier episode He questions the disciples' fear and stills the storm.
Both accounts describe the wind ceasing when Jesus enters the boat; Matthew also includes Peter in the plural they.
The boat occupants' confession that Jesus is God's Son corresponds to Peter's later confession of Him as the Christ and Son of the living God. The occasions and speakers differ.
Both describe the crossing ending with arrival at Gennesaret; Mark additionally records mooring the boat.
Both connect recognition of Jesus with people carrying the sick to Him throughout the surrounding region.
Both describe requests to touch the fringe of Jesus' garment and the healing or saving of those who touched Him.
Both introduce Pharisees and scribes who came from Jerusalem to Jesus.
Both record the objection that Jesus' disciples eat without following the elders' handwashing tradition.
Both contrast God's commandment with the opponents' adherence to or establishment of human tradition.
Both cite the commandments to honor father and mother and the death sanction for reviling a parent. Matthew introduces them as what God said; Mark as what Moses said.
Both describe declaring resources that could benefit a parent to be a gift. Mark additionally supplies and translates the term Corban.
Both describe the resulting failure to help or honor parents as nullifying God's word through tradition.
Both call the opponents hypocrites and introduce Isaiah's prophecy as apt to them; Mark also begins the citation in the same verse.
Matthew quotes Isaiah's contrast between honoring God with the lips and keeping the heart far away; Isaiah's fuller verse also describes drawing near and vain reverence.
Both describe vain worship or reverence associated with teaching human commands; the supplied Isaiah text says human commands and teachings.
Both describe Jesus summoning the crowd and telling them to listen and understand.
Both distinguish what enters a person from what comes out, locating defilement in what comes out; Matthew explicitly speaks of the mouth.

Matthew uses uprooting for plants not planted by the heavenly Father; John identifies the Father as vinegrower and describes Him removing fruitless branches. Both portray the Father's discriminating action through plant imagery, without identifying plants and branches as the same parable.
Both use a blind guide leading another blind person into a pit; Matthew applies the image to the guides being discussed, while Luke frames it as a question.
Both record a private request to explain the defilement parable. Matthew names Peter as the requester; Mark describes the disciples asking after entering a house.
Both open Jesus' explanation by questioning the disciples' continued lack of understanding.
Both explain the physical route of food through the stomach into the latrine; Mark additionally contrasts the heart and appends a statement about cleansing all foods.
Both identify defilement with what comes from within a person, specifically the heart, rather than with ingested food.

Both list evils originating in the heart, including murders, adulteries, sexual immorality, and thefts. The lists differ in length and some terminology, so their individual items are not forced into exact equivalence.
Both conclude that evil things originating within defile the person; Matthew additionally returns explicitly to the issue of eating with unwashed hands.
Both place Jesus' withdrawal in the territory of Tyre; Matthew also names Sidon, whereas Mark adds His desire to remain unnoticed in a house.
Both describe a woman petitioning Jesus for a demon-afflicted daughter. Matthew calls her Canaanite and records her address Lord, Son of David; Mark calls her Greek and Syrophoenician by birth.

Jesus' statement that He was sent to Israel's lost sheep corresponds to His earlier instruction sending the Twelve to those same lost sheep. The statements concern His mission and the disciples' mission respectively.
Both describe the woman approaching and bowing or falling at Jesus' feet; Matthew records the words Lord, help me, while Mark's cited verse does not reproduce that plea.
Both use the contrast between children's bread and little dogs in Jesus' answer; Mark additionally says the children should first be satisfied.
Both replies appeal to the little dogs eating crumbs under or from the table. Matthew describes crumbs falling from their masters' table; Mark calls them the children's crumbs.

Both describe Jesus granting the woman's request and her daughter being delivered. Matthew expressly praises her great faith and states healing from that hour; Mark connects the response to her words and describes her finding the child delivered at home.
Both travel notices move from the Tyre-Sidon region to the Sea of Galilee. Mark includes passage through the Decapolis; Matthew additionally describes ascent of a mountain and sitting there.

The crowd's bringing blind and lame people for healing corresponds to Jesus' earlier account of the blind receiving sight and the lame walking. The other conditions in the two lists differ, and the report does not describe this same gathering.

Matthew's restored sight, walking, and speech recall Isaiah's promised opening of blind eyes, the lame leaping, and clear speech. This compares the restoration imagery without claiming that every detail, including Isaiah's wilderness water, is narrated here.
Both describe Jesus' compassion for a crowd that has remained three days without food and His concern that dismissing them fasting would cause collapse on the road.
Both give the disciples' question about obtaining enough bread in a deserted place to satisfy the crowd.
Both record Jesus asking how many loaves are available and the answer seven; Matthew also mentions a few small fish, which Mark reports later.
Both describe Jesus ordering the crowd to recline on the ground before distributing the food.
Both describe seven loaves being blessed or given thanks over, broken, and distributed through the disciples, with small fish also provided; Mark describes the fish blessing separately.
Both report everyone eating to satisfaction and seven large baskets or hampers of leftover pieces being collected.
Both count about four thousand eaters; Matthew specifies men besides women and children, while Mark calls them people.

Both follow the crowd's dismissal with Jesus' boat journey. Matthew names the territory of Magadan and Mark the district of Dalmanutha; the names are preserved without asserting that the saved records establish their geographical identity.
Both describe opponents testing Jesus by requesting a sign from heaven. Matthew names Pharisees and Sadducees; Mark names Pharisees.

Both teachings contrast successful weather assessment with failure to assess the present time. Matthew uses a red evening sky, whereas Luke uses a western cloud and south wind; these are different weather examples.
Both rebuke those who can assess the sky's appearance but fail to discern the significance of the present time.
Both responses describe an evil and adulterous generation seeking a sign and allow only the sign of Jonah; this is a repeated saying in different settings within Matthew.
Both describe the disciples forgetting to bring bread for the boat journey. Mark additionally says there was one loaf in the boat.
Both warn the disciples against the leaven of the Pharisees. Matthew additionally names the Sadducees; Mark instead names Herod, so the additional referents are not equated.
Both describe the disciples interpreting Jesus' warning through their failure to bring bread.
Both describe Jesus recognizing their discussion about lacking bread and questioning their failure to understand; Matthew calls them people of little faith, whereas Mark asks about a hardened heart.
Both recall the five loaves for the five thousand and the baskets of fragments collected afterward; Mark supplies the disciples' answer twelve.
Both recall the seven loaves for the four thousand and the large baskets collected; Mark supplies the disciples' answer seven.

Both narratives juxtapose the leaven warning with the disciples' mistaken discussion of missing bread and Jesus' challenge to their understanding. Matthew names Pharisees and Sadducees, while Mark names Pharisees and Herod.

Both explain Pharisaic leaven as something beyond literal bread. Matthew identifies the teaching of Pharisees and Sadducees; Luke identifies the Pharisees' hypocrisy, so the interpretations are compared rather than made identical.
Both locate Jesus' question about public judgments of His identity near Caesarea Philippi; Matthew phrases it as the identity of the Son of Man and Mark as His own identity.
Both report identifications of Jesus as John the Baptist, Elijah, or a prophet. Matthew additionally names Jeremiah.
Both record Jesus turning the identity question directly to the disciples: who do you say I am?
Both record Peter confessing Jesus as the Christ. Matthew's confession additionally calls Him the Son of the living God.

Jesus attributes Peter's recognition to the heavenly Father's revelation rather than flesh and blood; the earlier thanksgiving likewise attributes understanding to the Father's revealing action and speaks of knowledge of the Son. These are different sayings about revelation.

Both connect Simon with the name Peter: Matthew addresses him as Peter while making the Church promise, and John records Jesus naming Simon Cephas and explicitly translating that name as Peter. John does not repeat the rock, Church, or Hades promises.

Both sayings connect earthly binding and loosing with heavenly binding and loosing. Here Jesus addresses Peter and also promises kingdom keys; Matthew 18:18 addresses a plural audience and does not mention keys.
Both follow Peter's confession with Jesus directing the disciples not to tell others about Him; Matthew expressly identifies the concealed confession as His being the Christ.

Both predict rejection or suffering involving elders, chief priests, and scribes, followed by death and resurrection. Matthew says on the third day and Mark after three days; that wording distinction is retained.
Both describe Peter taking Jesus aside and rebuking Him after the suffering prediction. Matthew supplies Peter's protest; Mark does not reproduce its words.
Both record Jesus addressing Peter as Satan and contrasting human concerns with God's concerns. Matthew additionally calls Peter a stumbling block.
Both require a would-be follower to deny himself, take up his cross, and follow Jesus. Matthew addresses the disciples; Mark includes the crowd with the disciples.
Both contrast losing life through seeking to save it with finding or saving life through losing it for Jesus. Mark additionally mentions the gospel.
Both ask what benefit there is in gaining the world while forfeiting life and what a person can give in exchange for life.

Matthew's promise to repay each person according to conduct recalls the psalm's address to the Lord that He will repay each according to works. Matthew applies the repayment to the Son of Man's coming with angels; those additional details are not in this psalm verse.

Both promise that some present will not taste death before seeing the kingdom's arrival or manifestation. Matthew speaks of the Son of Man coming in His kingdom, and Mark of God's kingdom having come in power; the link does not assign a date or a single interpretive fulfillment.
Both place Jesus' private ascent of a high mountain with Peter, James, and John after six days.

Both describe Jesus' transfiguration and brilliantly white clothing; Matthew additionally describes His face shining like the sun, while Mark compares the clothing with what no earthly bleacher could whiten.
Both report Moses and Elijah appearing and conversing with Jesus; the named order differs.
Both record Peter saying it is good to be there and proposing three tents, one each for Jesus, Moses, and Elijah. Matthew addresses Jesus as Lord and Mark as Rabbi.

Both describe the overshadowing cloud and the voice identifying Jesus as the beloved Son and commanding the hearers to listen to Him. Matthew additionally describes a bright cloud and divine pleasure in Him.

Both transfiguration accounts describe the disciples' fear. Matthew places their falling on their faces in response to the voice; Mark mentions terror while explaining Peter's proposal, so the precise placement is not harmonized.

Jesus' touch, instruction to rise, and reassurance not to fear after the vision resemble Daniel's being raised by a hand and told to stand and not fear. The actors and visions differ; the link does not identify Daniel's messenger as Jesus.
Both conclude the appearance of Moses and Elijah with the disciples looking and seeing Jesus alone.
Both describe the descent from the mountain and Jesus' prohibition on reporting what they saw until the Son of Man's resurrection.
Both record the disciples asking why the scribes say Elijah must come first.
Both record Jesus affirming Elijah's coming and restoration of all things; Mark joins this to a question about the Son of Man's suffering and contempt.

Both say Elijah has already come and was subjected to what others wished. Matthew additionally states that he was not recognized and explicitly parallels his treatment with the Son of Man's coming suffering.

The disciples' recognition that Jesus spoke about John the Baptist corresponds to Jesus' earlier identification of John as the Elijah who is to come. This connects the supplied narrative's own identification, without treating John and the historical Elijah as the same ordinary human individual.
Both introduce the afflicted boy's father approaching from the crowd and petitioning Jesus; Matthew describes his kneeling and Luke his calling out about his only son.

Both fathers describe the boy's repeated danger from fire and water and appeal for compassionate help. Matthew calls his condition seizures; Mark's surrounding narrative attributes the attacks to the spirit.
Both report that the father brought the boy or his request to the disciples, who were unable to cast out the spirit or heal him.
Both record Jesus lamenting the unbelieving generation, asking how long He must remain and bear with them, and commanding that the boy be brought to Him.
Both describe Jesus rebuking the demon or unclean spirit and healing the boy; Luke also narrates the convulsion during his approach and his return to his father.
Both record the disciples privately asking Jesus why they could not cast out the spirit.

Both use faith like a mustard seed to illustrate an apparently impossible command becoming effective. Matthew names a mountain moving from here to there; Luke names a mulberry tree uprooted and planted in the sea. The images and settings differ.
Both place a prediction of the Son of Man being handed over into human hands in a Galilean setting; Mark describes passing through Galilee and continues into the death and resurrection prediction.
Both predict killing and resurrection after the betrayal saying. Matthew says on the third day and describes grief; Mark says after three days and describes incomprehension and fear of asking.

Jesus arranges payment to avoid causing others to stumble, while Paul describes forgoing a right to avoid hindering the gospel. The shared principle is voluntary restraint for others' sake; Paul's passage does not parallel the fish or coin miracle.

deferred.reason: The instruction not to uproot wheat while gathering darnel was read. The later parable explanation identifies the plants and final harvest but does not closely restate this particular warning about premature removal; no separate passage was retained for it in this batch.

The scribe-householder bringing new and old treasures was read. No sufficiently close independent target was established for this distinctive comparison; general references to scribes, wisdom, or treasure would not adequately explain its particular claim.
The departure notice after the parables was read. Similar travel transitions were considered too general to count as a supported cross-reference for this source unit.

Jesus' command to bring the five loaves and two fish to Him was read. The other feeding accounts describe the food's availability and Jesus taking it but do not closely reproduce this distinctive command; no retained target was established for this unit.

Peter's conditional request for Jesus to command him onto the water was read. Mark and John's sea-walking accounts do not include Peter's request, and a separate sufficiently specific target was not established.

Peter's stepping from the boat and walking toward Jesus at His command was read. The other sea-walking accounts do not include this action; generic references to following Jesus or walking through water were not counted.

The disciples' report that the Pharisees took offense at the defilement saying was read. Mark's parallel discourse does not include this report, and unrelated offense passages were not retained merely for shared vocabulary.
Jesus' initial silence and the disciples' request to dismiss the crying woman were read. Mark's account does not reproduce these features; no sufficiently specific alternative passage was retained.

The collectors' question about the didrachmas was read. Exodus 30:13–15 was examined, but its supplied wording specifies a half-didrachma census contribution and does not establish the identity or amount of this collection. The levy identification and source wording need further substantive review before retaining that candidate.
Peter's reply and Jesus' question about whether earthly kings collect from sons or strangers were read. No sufficiently close independent target was established for this distinctive fiscal analogy.
The conclusion that the sons are free was read in its tax-discussion context. General sayings about spiritual freedom were not counted as equivalent to this particular argument about royal taxation.

review_notes: Read every original source unit in Matthew chapters 13–17 from the exact pinned Saints English source. The inventory contains 187 units; Matthew 17:21 is absent in the supplied source and was not invented or imported.

Read all retained target passages directly in the exact Saints cache. Target ranges preserve original order and numbering, including Psalms 77:2, Psalms 61:13, and the supplied Greek-based Daniel 12:3 wording.

Same-chapter parable-and-explanation links are explicit: the darnel images in Matthew 13:24–30 are connected with their explanations at 13:37–43. Repeated judgment language and related kingdom parables are separately labelled thematic parallels. These do not claim independent narrative attestation.

Matthew 13:13 and Mark 4:12 use different causal wording for parables. Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3 differ over craftsman's son/carpenter and Joseph/Joses. Matthew 14:6 and the supplied Mark 6:22 differ in the dancer's description. These differences were stated without harmonization.
Matthew's Magadan and Mark's Dalmanutha were preserved as distinct saved names; geographical equivalence was not asserted. Sadducees and Herod in the leaven warnings were not equated.

The transfiguration reassurance comparison with Daniel 10 is thematic and does not identify the figures. The John-as-Elijah link follows Matthew's own stated identification and does not merge ordinary historical identities.
Eleven reviewed source units remain deferred with zero completion credit. They require further substantive passage review; the numerical target does not justify generic or unsupported matches.
Source wording, original IDs, chapter divisions, absent-verse gaps, display wording and continuation paragraphs are unchanged by these proposals.
